draft.title: Caring for heritage and ancestral remains
card: Ancestral remains are the bodies of First Nations people who lived long ago. Sacred sites are places of spiritual importance. Both are part of the heritage of living communities today.
Because they belong to living communities, researchers need the consent of the community before they study remains or sites. Science alone does not give them the right.
In the past, many ancestral remains were taken from Country and held in museums and universities. Communities have long asked for their return.
Mungo Man was found at Lake Mungo in New South Wales. His remains were returned to Country in 2017, after decades of advocacy by Traditional Owners.
draft.remember: Heritage belongs to living communities, so their consent comes first.

a.q: Why do researchers need consent from a community before studying ancestral remains?
opts: The remains belong to living communities, not researchers
The remains are too old to be studied by scientists
The remains have already been fully studied by museums
The remains can only be studied by people in that community
a.why: Ancestral remains are part of the heritage of living communities, so the community decides whether research goes ahead. Age is not the reason. The card says researchers need consent, not that nobody else may ever study them.
a.clue: Think about who the remains belong to today.

b.q: A university holds ancestral remains taken from a river region long ago. Traditional Owners ask for them to be returned to Country. What does the Mungo Man example suggest about this request?
opts: Return can follow decades of advocacy by the community
Return happens quickly once a community asks for it
Return is decided by the museum that holds the remains
Return is only possible if scientists finish their research
b.why: Mungo Man's remains were returned in 2017 after decades of advocacy by Traditional Owners. This shows that return can take a long time and a lot of effort. It was not quick, and it was not left to the holders of the remains.
b.clue: Look at how long the Mungo Man return took.

a.best: The remains belong to living communities, not researchers

b.best: Return can follow decades of advocacy by the community

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a soft qualifier ("can") and it repeats the card's exact phrase "decades of advocacy". The three distractors are all absolute or flat claims ("only possible if", "is decided by", "happens quickly"). A student could pick it without knowing the idea, and the clue about how long the return took points straight at it.

The why says the return "was not left to the holders of the remains", but the card says nothing about who decided. That makes the distractor "Return is decided by the museum that holds the remains" wrong on grounds the card does not teach.

check.summary: The facts check out: Mungo Man was found at Lake Mungo in NSW and returned to Country in 2017. In question b the right option stands out as the only hedged one and copies the card's wording, and its why claims more than the card says about who decided the return.

a.why: Ancestral remains are part of the heritage of living communities, so the community decides whether research goes ahead. Age is not the reason. The card says researchers need consent, not that nobody else may ever study them.
a.clue: Think about who the remains belong to today.

b.q: Sam reads that Mungo Man was found in 1974 and returned to Country in 2017. Which statement fits what happened?
opts: Traditional Owners pushed for his return over many years
He was returned within a year of being found in 1974
He was kept away from Country because researchers owned him
He was returned to Country without his community asking
b.why: More than 40 years passed between 1974 and 2017, and his return followed decades of advocacy by Traditional Owners. The idea that researchers owned him is wrong, because ancestral remains belong to living communities, and he was returned.
b.clue: Who did the card say spoke up for his return?
